question.text: An anchor LP of 'Brahmaputra Infra AIF' negotiates a 'Most Favoured Nation' (MFN) clause in its side letter. What does an MFN clause primarily allow the investor to do?

answer.text: Receive side letter entitlements that protect against less favourable terms/conditions compared to those offered to other current or future investors
Redeem units before the lock-in period without paying exit load
Get a guaranteed minimum IRR of the hurdle rate
Demand appointment of the investor's nominee as the trustee

explanation.text: The Logic: Per Section 13.4.1 and footnote 130, an MFN clause allows an investor to receive side letter entitlements, which can be used to protect themselves from less favourable terms or conditions in the PPM as compared to the terms or conditions offered to other current or future investors. It's parity protection, not redemption or return protection. The Trap: MFN is often confused with lock-in waivers or return guarantees — it is purely a parity mechanism. It is NOT a return guarantee or a governance right. Cross-Exam Context: XIX-A covers MFN at recall level. XIX-C manager-side requires knowledge of how MFN is operationalised (election mechanism, carve-outs for ticket size, regulatory status etc.). Manager's Pro-Tip: When granting MFN, carve out: (a) side letter terms tied to regulatory status of LP, (b) terms tied to AUM/ticket size, (c) terms tied to jurisdiction-specific tax — else you create unmanageable waterfall complexity at close of fund.
